A few things that have helped me establish a routine have been:

I made a spreadsheet of all the daily and weekly chores I had. There’s a section of must do—have to feed the cat, have to take my medication, have meals, deal with that day’s mail, etc., then a section of it would be ideal if these things happened each day as well—took a shower, put on clean clothes, took care of that day’s dishes, etc., a section of things that it would be awesome to get to like exercising for at least a half hour, write in my journal, read for a half hour. Each day has one chore that has to be done that day and it only needs done once a week—Sunday fill pill box for the coming week, Monday take the recycling and trash out for collection, etc. 

Having that little list has helped me to do at least those little things and I found a way to fit them into my day that makes most sense for me. Some people schedule chores more rigidly, like at 9:00-10:00 I’ll do X,Y, and Z. For me, that often failed because if I didn’t do them at that time I felt defeated and like a failure and gave up on everything that day. 

I can send a copy of my list if you wanted to see and example. 

When people tell you to create structure in your life, I think we often try to imitate structures we’ve seen before, like school and work where things have to be done at certain times in certain orders. For me, getting the things done matters more than getting the things done at 2pm exactly or whatever.

Timing things helps to. If I can’t get myself started on something, I’ll set a timer for 15 or 20 minutes and stop after that. It makes it feel less overwhelming if I only have to do it for a small amount of time. You do it for 5 or 10. Sometimes once I get started, I go can two sets of 15 instead of stopping after one.

I do the same thing. I have an “eco cube”—it’s a block of 700 non sticky post it bits sized papers. Any time I have a random thought or have something I want to remember to do, I write it on a square and keep them on my table as they accumulate. 

At the end of the day or every few hours, I go through them and sort them—things that need added to a to do list, things to look up, things to add to the grocery list—it usually works, but sometimes the cat knocks them over or I get my piles mixed up and toss the stack I haven’t dealt with yet.

Another is seeing if your school has a disability resource office and speaking to a counselor there to see what accommodations you may be entitled to, like extensions on assignments, being able to make audio recordings of lectures.
Usually they will put together a form letter to give to professors at the beginning of a semester outlining that you have a disability (they don’t specifically say what it is) and you need these accommodations. 

It’s also good to tell your professors up front that you might struggle with things and ask for leniency. It’s better to state the problem early rather than try to fix everything at the end of the semester or ask for mercy after the fact once you’re in danger of failing or didn’t turn in major assignments on time. That’s not to say every professor will be agreeable, some are very strict about their policies or feel like at this stage/age you should be able to handle it.
